claims.text: The baseline platinum-group metal nanoscale catalyst has a largely metallic surface.
Mild oxygen exposure can induce partial surface oxidation of the catalyst.
The induced partially oxidized surface is stable under the stated operating conditions.
Controlled moderate surface oxidation changes the binding strength of ethanol-oxidation intermediates.
Partial oxidation increases selectivity toward complete 12-electron ethanol oxidation.
Partial oxidation improves long-term catalyst durability by reducing deactivation by poisoning species.
Partial oxidation forms surface oxide species or oxygen vacancies.
Surface oxide species or oxygen vacancies tune the catalyst's electronic properties.
Changes in the catalyst's electronic properties modify the adsorption energies of key reaction intermediates.
Partial oxidation makes strongly binding intermediates such as adsorbed CO bind neither too strongly nor too weakly.
Intermediate binding of optimal strength minimizes catalyst poisoning.
Intermediate binding of optimal strength promotes the complete 12-electron ethanol-oxidation pathway.
Reduced poisoning maintains active sites during electrochemical cycling.
The partially oxidized catalyst will have a higher current density than the pristine metallic catalyst.
The partially oxidized catalyst will produce a greater proportion of complete-oxidation products than the pristine catalyst.
The partially oxidized catalyst will retain performance better over extended cycling than the pristine catalyst.
The proposed behavior applies under moderate oxygen partial pressures, ambient temperature, and acidic conditions.
Extreme reducing or oxidizing conditions may create alternative surface states and eliminate the predicted behavior.
